title: Prototypes & `this`: The JavaScript Binding Handbook
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on how JavaScript really resolves properties and function context — the prototype chain, `__proto__` vs `prototype`, explicit binding with call/apply/bind, arrow-function lexical `this`, and what `class` desugars into. Covers internals, practical patterns, performance trade-offs, and the classic gotchas that break real code.

chapters.title: Objects Without Classes: Why Prototypes Exist
points: JavaScript has no classical inheritance at runtime — objects delegate to other objects; `class` is syntax over this delegation
Definition: a prototype is an ordinary object that another object links to for failed property lookups
Every object has an internal slot `[[Prototype]]`, spec-notated as such; `__proto__` and `Object.getPrototypeOf` are its accessors
Delegation vs copying: `const b = Object.create(a)` links b to a; mutating `a.x` later is visible through `b.x` — copying with spread would not be
Object literals get `Object.prototype` as `[[Prototype]]` by default; that's the source of `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`
`Object.create(null)` makes a null-prototype object — no inherited members, safe as a pure dictionary/map, but `obj.toString()` throws
Functions get `Function.prototype`, arrays get `Array.prototype`, so `[].map` is inherited, not own
Own vs inherited: `Object.hasOwn(o,'k')` / `o.hasOwnProperty('k')` is true only for own props; `'k' in o` walks the whole chain
Mental model: property lookup is a linked-list walk; property assignment (usually) is not
Prototypes make method sharing memory-cheap: 10,000 instances, one copy of each method

chapters.title: The Prototype Chain: Lookup Mechanics
points: Read algorithm: check own properties, else follow `[[Prototype]]`, repeat until `null`, then yield `undefined` (no ReferenceError)
Chain example: `const a = [1]` gives `a → Array.prototype → Object.prototype → null`
Shadowing: an own property with the same name hides the prototype's version; `delete o.k` un-shadows and reveals the inherited one again
Write algorithm differs: `o.k = v` creates an OWN property on `o` even when `k` exists up-chain — it does not mutate the prototype
Exception to the above: if an inherited property is an accessor with a setter, assignment CALLS that setter instead of creating an own prop
Second exception: an inherited non-writable data property makes `o.k = v` silently fail (throws in strict mode)
Methods called via the chain still get `this` = the receiver object, not the prototype that owns the method — that's what makes delegation useful
`Object.getPrototypeOf(o)` reads the link; `Object.setPrototypeOf(o, p)` writes it (slow — deoptimizes; prefer `Object.create`)
`for...in` enumerates own AND inherited enumerable string keys; `Object.keys` returns own enumerable only
Chain depth is a real cost: each miss walks one more object — deep chains slow property misses
`instanceof` walks the chain: `x instanceof C` is true if `C.prototype` appears anywhere in x's chain
Cycles are illegal: `Object.setPrototypeOf(a, b)` when `b` already inherits from `a` throws a TypeError

chapters.title: `__proto__` vs `prototype`: The Two Words People Confuse
points: `prototype` is a property ONLY on functions; `__proto__` is a link on every object — different things, similar names
`fn.prototype` is not fn's own prototype — it's the object that will become `[[Prototype]]` of instances created by `new fn()`
Invariant to memorize: `Object.getPrototypeOf(new Dog()) === Dog.prototype`
`Dog.__proto__ === Function.prototype` — a function's own prototype is Function.prototype, not `Dog.prototype`
`Dog.prototype.constructor === Dog` by default; overwriting `Dog.prototype = {...}` wholesale destroys that link, so restore `constructor` explicitly
`__proto__` is a legacy accessor defined on `Object.prototype` (Annex B, web-compat only) — prefer `Object.getPrototypeOf` / `Object.setPrototypeOf`
Because `__proto__` is a setter, `JSON.parse` and naive object merges can hit prototype pollution: a key `"__proto__"` in untrusted data
Null-prototype objects have no `__proto__` accessor at all — `Object.create(null).__proto__` is just a plain data key
Arrow functions, methods in object literals, and `class` methods have NO `prototype` property — they cannot be `new`ed
Table row: `Function.prototype.__proto__ === Object.prototype`, and `Object.prototype.__proto__ === null` (chain root)
Wiring diagram to memorize: instance → Ctor.prototype → Object.prototype → null, with Ctor.__proto__ → Function.prototype off to the side

chapters.title: Constructor Functions and What `new` Actually Does
points: The four steps of `new Fn(args)`: create empty object; set its `[[Prototype]]` to `Fn.prototype`; call `Fn` with `this` = that object; return it unless the body returns an object
Return override rule: `return {a:1}` from a constructor replaces the instance; returning a primitive is ignored
Idiomatic pattern: assign per-instance state in the constructor body, shared methods on `Fn.prototype`
Code: `function Dog(n){this.name=n} Dog.prototype.speak=function(){return this.name+' barks'}`
Forgetting `new` on a plain function: `this` is `undefined` in strict mode (TypeError on assignment) or the global object in sloppy mode — silent global leak
`new.target` is `undefined` on a normal call and the constructor on a `new` call — use it to guard or auto-`new`
Manual prototypal inheritance before `class`: `Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype)` then reset `Child.prototype.constructor = Child`
Parent constructor chaining by hand: `Parent.call(this, args)` inside `Child`
Why `Child.prototype = new Parent()` is the wrong old idiom: it runs the parent constructor early and leaks its instance fields onto the shared prototype
`Object.create(proto, descriptors)` builds a linked object without calling any constructor
Factory-function alternative: return a literal with closures — no `this`, no `new`, but a copy of each method per instance

chapters.title: How `this` Gets Its Value: The Binding Rules
points: Core rule: `this` in a normal function is determined by the CALL SITE, not where the function was defined
Rule 1 — default binding: standalone `f()` gives `undefined` in strict mode / modules, globalThis in sloppy mode
Rule 2 — implicit binding: `obj.f()` sets `this` to `obj`; only the LAST dot before the call counts (`a.b.f()` gives `b`)
Rule 3 — explicit binding: `f.call(obj)`, `f.apply(obj)`, `f.bind(obj)` set `this` directly
Rule 4 — `new` binding: `new F()` sets `this` to the freshly created object
Precedence order: `new` > explicit (bind) > implicit (dot) > default
Arrow functions sit outside this list entirely — they have no `this` of their own
Lost binding: `const f = obj.method; f()` drops the receiver — the classic callback bug
`this` in a getter/setter is the object the property was accessed on, i.e. the receiver, not the definer
`this` at module top level is `undefined` in ESM; `module.exports` in CJS; `globalThis` in a classic script
DOM handlers set `this` to the element for `function` listeners — but an arrow listener keeps outer `this` (use `event.currentTarget` instead)

chapters.title: call, apply, and bind
points: `fn.call(thisArg, a, b)` — invoke now, arguments listed individually
`fn.apply(thisArg, [a, b])` — invoke now, arguments as an array-like; mnemonic: A for Array
`fn.bind(thisArg, a)` — invoke never; returns a NEW function permanently bound, with optional partial application of leading args
Bound functions are hard-bound: a later `.call(other)` on the result is ignored — rebinding a bound function does nothing
But `new` DOES override a bound `this` (though bound leading arguments are still prepended)
`bind` returns a new function object each call — `el.removeEventListener('x', fn.bind(o))` never removes anything; store the bound reference
Partial application: `const add5 = add.bind(null, 5)`
Method borrowing: `Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)` to array-ify array-likes; `[].map.call(nodeList, f)`
Type check idiom: `Object.prototype.toString.call(x)` returns `"[object Array]"`, `"[object Null]"`, etc.
In sloppy mode `call(null)` / `call(undefined)` substitutes globalThis, and primitives get boxed to objects; strict mode passes them through untouched
Modern replacements: spread `fn(...args)` instead of `apply`; `Reflect.apply(fn, thisArg, args)` for a non-borrowable path
Cost note: `bind` allocates — avoid creating bound functions inside render loops or hot paths

chapters.title: Arrow Functions and Lexical `this`
points: Arrows have no `this` binding — `this` resolves lexically up the scope chain, exactly like any other variable
Consequence: `call`, `apply`, `bind` cannot change an arrow's `this`; the thisArg is silently ignored
Fixes the callback problem: `setTimeout(() => this.tick(), 100)` keeps the enclosing `this`
Pre-arrow workarounds this replaced: `const self = this`, `.bind(this)`, and the `thisArg` second parameter of `forEach`/`map`
Arrows also lack their own `arguments`, `super`, and `new.target` — all lexical
Arrows have no `prototype` property and throw `TypeError: not a constructor` under `new`
Never use an arrow as an object-literal method: `{ name:'a', get(){ } }` works, `{ name:'a', get: () => this.name }` reads outer `this`
Never use an arrow for a prototype method that needs the instance — `Dog.prototype.speak = () => this.name` is broken for every instance
Class fields with arrows (`handle = () => {...}`) auto-bind per instance — costs one function per instance, and it's an own property, not on the prototype
So an arrow class field is not on the prototype: it can't be called via `super`, and it shadows a same-named prototype method
Rule of thumb: arrow for callbacks and short lexical closures; `function`/method shorthand when the call site should supply `this`

chapters.title: `class` Desugared
points: `class C {}` creates a function object; `typeof C === 'function'` — it is prototype machinery with better ergonomics
Methods in a class body land on `C.prototype`, non-enumerable, so `for...in` over an instance won't list them (unlike hand-written prototype assignment)
`static` members land on the constructor `C` itself, not on `C.prototype`
`extends` wires two links: `Child.prototype.__proto__ = Parent.prototype` (instance methods) AND `Child.__proto__ = Parent` (static inheritance)
Static inheritance is the part manual ES5 patterns usually forgot — `class` gives it for free
`super.method()` is not `this.__proto__.method()` — it uses the method's `[[HomeObject]]`, which is why extracted methods can still resolve `super`
`super(args)` in a derived constructor is what actually CREATES `this`; touching `this` before it throws a ReferenceError
Class bodies are always strict mode, and class declarations are hoisted but in the temporal dead zone (`new C()` before the declaration throws)
Classes cannot be called without `new` — `C()` throws a TypeError, unlike constructor functions
Instance fields (`x = 1`) are own properties initialized per instance, in order, before the constructor body's statements run
Private fields `#x` are NOT prototype properties or hidden conventions — real per-instance slots, unreachable via the chain or reflection
Getters/setters in a class body become accessor descriptors on `C.prototype`

chapters.title: Trade-offs: Prototypes vs Closures vs Classes
points: Memory: prototype methods = 1 function per class; closure/factory methods and arrow class fields = 1 function per instance
Property access speed: own property is fastest; each chain hop adds lookup work on a miss — engines mitigate via inline caches and hidden classes
Megamorphic penalty: mutating shapes or prototypes after creation invalidates inline caches — `Object.setPrototypeOf` in hot code is the classic deopt
Encapsulation: closures give true privacy cheaply; `#private` fields give privacy with prototype-level method sharing
Ergonomics: `class` gets `extends`, `super`, static inheritance, and better stack traces/devtools output
Factories compose (mixins, object spread) where single-`[[Prototype]]` inheritance cannot — JS has no multiple inheritance
Mixin pattern: `Object.assign(C.prototype, behaviorObj)` copies methods, losing the delegation link (no live updates)
Composition over deep inheritance: 4+ level chains hurt both performance and comprehension
`Object.freeze(C.prototype)` locks shared methods; frozen prototypes make monkey-patching fail silently in sloppy mode
Guidance: `class` for entities with identity and inheritance; factories/closures for stateful units and privacy; plain objects + functions for data

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Passing a method as a callback: `arr.forEach(this.handler)` loses `this` — pass `this.handler.bind(this)` or an arrow wrapper
`setTimeout(obj.method, 0)` — same lost binding, plus browsers set `this` to `window` for the timer callback
Arrow in a prototype/object method — `this` is the module or window, not the instance
Putting mutable state on a prototype: `Dog.prototype.toys = []` is SHARED by all instances, so `push` mutates it for everyone
Assigning `C.prototype = {...}` and wiping `constructor`; also breaks any instances already created against the old prototype object
`for...in` picking up inherited props from a modified `Object.prototype` — guard with `Object.hasOwn` or use `Object.keys`
Prototype pollution: merging untrusted JSON with a `__proto__` or `constructor.prototype` key mutates `Object.prototype` globally — reject those keys or use null-prototype targets
`instanceof` fails across realms (iframes, worker/vm contexts) — different `Array.prototype`; use `Array.isArray` or `Symbol.hasInstance`
`typeof null === 'object'` and `Object.prototype.toString.call(null)` — null has no prototype, `null.x` throws
Overriding `bind` results: expecting `boundFn.call(other)` to rebind (it won't) — hard-bound is permanent
Extracting a class method and calling it bare throws a TypeError (class bodies are strict, so `this` is `undefined`) — a silent bug in sloppy code
Forgetting `super()` in a derived constructor, or using `this` before it — ReferenceError, not `undefined`

chapters.title: Summary & Quick Reference
points: One-line rule 1: `prototype` belongs to functions and defines what instances inherit; `__proto__`/`[[Prototype]]` is what an object actually inherits from
One-line rule 2: reads walk the chain, writes create own properties (unless a setter or non-writable prop intervenes)
One-line rule 3: for `function`s, `this` comes from the call site; for arrows, from the enclosing lexical scope
Binding precedence recap: `new` > `bind`/`call`/`apply` > `obj.f()` > default (`undefined` in strict)
Decision table: change `this` now with one arg list → `call`; now with an array → `apply`; later/permanently → `bind`; never → arrow
Inspect at the console: `Object.getPrototypeOf(x)`, `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(C.prototype)`, `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(o,'k')`, `x.constructor.name`
Debug checklist for `this === undefined`: was the method extracted, was it passed as a callback, is it an arrow, is it strict mode
Safety checklist: never store mutable state on a prototype; never `setPrototypeOf` in hot paths; never trust `__proto__` keys from user input
Modern defaults: `class` + `#private` fields for entities, arrow class fields for handler auto-binding, spread instead of `apply`
The whole model in one sentence: objects delegate property lookups up a chain of objects, and functions receive `this` from how they are called
